title: Understanding Teacher Perspectives and Experiences After Deployment of AI Literacy Curriculum in Middle-School Classrooms
extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school teachers experienced the implementation of a new AI literacy curriculum, RAICA (Responsible AI for Computational Action), and how their beliefs about AI and teaching changed after classroom deployment. The study is motivated by a gap in K-12 AI education research: prior work has often focused on researchers as instructors, with less direct evidence from classroom teachers about what support they need to teach AI effectively.

The intervention consisted of three project-based RAICA modules taught in middle-school classrooms, supported by teacher guides, slides, student workbooks, assessments, a kanban planning board, ongoing professional development, and weekly debrief sessions with researchers. Seven teachers from interdisciplinary backgrounds (art, business, and computer science) implemented one module each and then participated in semi-structured remote interviews. The analysis is qualitative and thematic, based on eight recorded interviews.

The study found that the curriculum helped teachers build foundational AI understanding, think more critically about ethical and societal implications, and adapt lessons creatively for their own classrooms. Teachers valued the open-ended, flexible design and peer support, but also reported technical challenges, time constraints, and a need for more specific guidance, walkthroughs, and individualized support such as one-on-one code reviews. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher training, flexible materials, and continuous feedback are important for successful AI curriculum deployment in K-12 settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study with seven teachers and thematic coding, so it does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental credibility standards. It does, however, use a clear methodology and direct participant evidence from classroom implementation.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful but unquantified positive effects on teacher knowledge, engagement, and student project-based learning, alongside implementation burdens. Because no effect sizes or objective outcome metrics are reported, overall impact is unclear and best classified as modest/uncertain.

interventions.use_case: AI literacy curriculum implementation in middle-school classrooms (MIT RAICA modules) supported by teacher professional development, curriculum materials, and weekly debriefs; teachers used the materials to teach foundational AI concepts, ethics, and project-based AI making.

finding.finding_summary: Seven teachers reported that the RAICA AI literacy modules expanded their own knowledge of AI concepts and ethics and helped them teach foundational AI ideas to middle-school students. The paper is qualitative and does not report quantitative effect sizes; evidence comes from semi-structured interviews with 7 teachers (8 interviews total) describing improved comprehension, confidence, and classroom implementation.
finding.measure: Semi-structured teacher interviews about AI concept understanding, curriculum implementation, and perceived student learning

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described higher student engagement, enthusiasm, and playful learning during the AI curriculum modules, and noted that the curriculum piqued interest in AI careers and self-efficacy about participating in the field. The evidence is qualitative and based on teacher perceptions rather than direct student outcome measures.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student engagement, interest, and confidence during module implementation

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that students practiced collaboration, brainstorming, empathy, design thinking, and iterative problem-solving while completing project-based AI activities such as chatbot and app design. The study provides qualitative evidence of improved critical thinking and metacognitive reflection through prompting, peer feedback, and use of kanban boards, but no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview reports of student collaboration, design thinking, reflection, and problem-solving during project work

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the curriculum and PD supported implementation, but they also described substantial preparation time, technical troubleshooting, vague guides, and the need for one-on-one support and more tutorials. Several teachers said they dropped AI components or found planning tools and materials difficult to use, indicating mixed effects on planning speed and workload.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported planning time, preparation burden, and ease of curriculum implementation
